notes.22:13: The Greek reads "one ram" (krios heis) and transliterates the Hebrew word for thicket as a plant name, "a sabek bush."
notes.22:14: The place name "The Lord Has Seen" (Kyrios eiden) and the saying "On the mountain the Lord has appeared" (ophthe) echo Abraham's words in v. 8, where the verb rendered "will provide" (opsetai) literally means "will see."
notes.22:21: In vv. 21-24 the Greek preserves several distinct name forms that differ in consonants from the Hebrew: Ox (Uz), Baux (Buz), Chaszad (Chesed), Jeldaph (Jidlaph), Reera (Reumah), Tabek (Tebah), and Taam (Gaham).
notes.23:2: The Greek reads "city of Arbok" (corresponding to Hebrew Kiriath-arba) and adds the clarifying phrase "which is in the valley."
notes.23:9: The Greek translates the Hebrew name Machpelah literally as "the double cave" (also in vv. 17, 19); in v. 8 it spells Ephron's father's name "Saar" (Hebrew Zohar).
notes.23:13: The Greek text reads the second-person imperative "bury" (thapson) rather than the first-person "I will bury" (thapso) found in some manuscripts and the Hebrew.
notes.23:15: The Greek reads "for I have heard" rather than "listen to me," and states the price in "didrachmas" (two-drachma silver coins, also in v. 16), corresponding to Hebrew shekels.
notes.24:7: The Greek text reads "the God of heaven and the God of the earth" and "To you I will give this land, and to your seed" (adding "and the God of the earth" and "To you" compared with the Hebrew Masoretic Text), and explicitly names Isaac here as in verses 3 and 4.
notes.24:22: The Greek specifies plural "golden earrings, each a drachma in weight" (rather than a single nose ring weighing half a shekel as in the Hebrew text) and gives the weight of the two bracelets as "ten gold pieces."
notes.24:26: The Greek uses the participle eudokesas ("being well pleased"), whereas the Hebrew text reads "bowed his head."
notes.24:27: The Greek renders the divine attribute as dikaiosyne ("righteousness") rather than "mercy" or "lovingkindness," and has singular "brother" rather than plural "brothers."
notes.24:31: The Greek text reads the nominative eulogetos Kyrios ("blessed be the Lord") as an exclamation of praise, rather than the genitive "blessed of the Lord."
notes.24:36: The Greek specifies "one son" and reads the masculine pronoun "after he had grown old" (referring to Abraham), whereas the Hebrew text reads "after she was old."
notes.24:50: The Greek reads the accusative-dative pair kakon kalo ("evil for good") rather than "bad or good," and uses prostagma ("decree") for the matter proceeding from the Lord.
notes.24:59: The Greek reads ta hyparchonta autes ("her possessions"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "her nurse."
notes.24:62: The Greek adds "through the wilderness" and translates the place name Beer Lahai Roi as "the Well of Vision."
notes.25:3: The Septuagint includes Teman among Jokshan's sons and adds Reuel and Nabdeel to the sons of Dedan, also reading Datusieim where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Letushim (and similarly Thergama in v. 4 for Eldaah).
notes.25:18: The Septuagint reads Suel where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Shur, and renders Ishmael's settlement in the presence of his brethren with the verb "dwelt."
notes.25:27: Greek aplastos ("guileless" or "unfeigned") and "dwelling in a house" reflect the Septuagint's distinctive rendering of Jacob's character and abode (compared with "dwelling in tents" in the Masoretic Text).
notes.26:10: Greek agnoia ("ignorance") is used in the Septuagint to denote an unwitting offense or sin of ignorance, rendering the Hebrew term for guilt.
notes.26:12: The Septuagint reads "barley" (krithen), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants rendered as "measures" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.26:20: Here and in vv. 21-23 and 33, the Septuagint translates the well names into Greek (Injustice, Enmity, Broad Space, and Well of the Oath) rather than transliterating the Hebrew names Esek, Sitnah, Rehoboth, and Beersheba.
notes.26:32: The Septuagint reads "We have not found water," taking the Hebrew consonants read as "to him" in the Masoretic Text ("We have found water") as the negative particle "not."
notes.26:34: The Septuagint gives the names Beer and Masemmath (for Hebrew Beeri and Basemath) and identifies Elon as "the Hivite" rather than "the Hittite."
notes.27:12: Greek kataphronon ("showing contempt" or "despising") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "a mocker" or "deceiver."
notes.27:29: The Greek reads "rulers" (archontes) and "the sons of your father," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "peoples" and "the sons of your mother."
notes.27:36: Greek epterniken (literally "tripped by the heel," here rendered "supplanted") preserves the wordplay on the name Jacob.
notes.27:40: Greek henika ean katheles kai eklyseis uses katheles ("pull down" or "cast down") with kai introducing the result clause ("you shall loosen").
notes.28:3: The Greek reads "my God" (ho theos mou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "God Almighty" (El Shaddai).
notes.28:10: The Greek translates the place name Beersheba literally as "the Well of the Oath."
notes.28:13: The Greek adds "Do not be afraid" and uses epestērikto ("stood firmly upon it"), echoing esterigmene ("set firmly") in verse 12.
notes.28:14: The Greek reads "the sand of the sea" (instead of the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "dust of the earth") and lists the directions in the order west (literally "sea"), south, north, and east.
notes.28:19: The Greek translates Bethel literally as "House of God" and gives the city's earlier name as Oulammaus, a Septuagint-distinct form combining the Hebrew adverb "however" (ulam) with the place name Luz.
notes.29:1: The Greek text adds Jacob's explicit destination ("to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau"), which is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.29:6: The Greek places Rachel's arrival with her father's sheep in the narrator's voice already here ("While he was still speaking..."), before resuming the notice in verse 9, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text includes the mention of her approach within the shepherds' reply.
notes.29:12: Literally "brother of her father" (Greek adelphos, as also in verse 15), reflecting the broad Semitic usage of "brother" for a close male kinsman.
notes.29:20: This Greek critical text concludes after "seven years," without the additional clause found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Septuagint witnesses stating that the years seemed like a few days because of Jacob's love for Rachel.
notes.29:27: Greek ta hebdoma ("seven days" or "week," also in verse 28) refers to the traditional seven-day bridal celebration for Leah.
notes.30:8: The Greek reads "God has come to my aid, and I have contended with my sister," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "with mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister."
notes.30:15: The Greek renders Rachel's opening reply as "Not so" (Ouch houtos), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "Therefore."
notes.30:27: The Greek uses the potential expression "I would take an omen" (oionisamen an) and refers to "God" rather than the divine name found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.30:32: In the Greek text Jacob instructs Laban to have the sheep pass by and separate them, whereas in the Hebrew Masoretic Text Jacob speaks in the first person ("I will pass through... removing").
notes.30:42: The Greek reads "whenever the sheep gave birth" and contrasts "unmarked" (asema) with "marked" (episema) animals, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text contrasts feeble and strong flocks.
notes.31:7: The Septuagint reads "of the ten lambs" here (and "by ten ewe-lambs" in 31:41), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "ten times."
notes.31:13: The Greek text reads "in the place where you anointed a pillar to Me there," without the name Bethel found in the Hebrew text, and concludes with "and I will be with you."
notes.31:33: Following the Septuagint, Laban searches Leah's house first (rather than Jacob's) before searching the houses of Jacob, the two maidservants, and Rachel; the Greek renders the tents as "house" throughout.
notes.31:47: Rather than transliterating the Aramaic and Hebrew names Jegar-sahadutha and Galeed, the Septuagint translates them directly into Greek as "Witness Heap" and "Heap Bears Witness."
notes.31:49: The Septuagint translates the place name Mizpah into Greek as "The Vision," and rearranges the covenant verses (31:44–54) compared to the Hebrew text, so that verse 31:51 does not appear as a separate verse.
notes.32:2: The Septuagint numbering of chapter 32 begins one verse earlier than the Hebrew Masoretic Text (32:1 corresponds to 31:55), and 32:2 uniquely adds that Jacob lifted up his eyes and saw "an encampment of God encamped," leading into the Greek translation of Mahanaim as Parembolai ("Encampments") in 32:3.
notes.32:11: The Greek source reads hikanousai moi ("You are sufficient for me"; other Greek witnesses read hikanoutai moi, "it is sufficient for me"), differing from the Hebrew "I am not worthy of all the mercies and all the truth."
notes.32:29: The final Greek clause omits the verb (literally "and with men mighty"), here rendered "and with men you shall be mighty."
notes.32:31: The Greek renders the Hebrew place name Peniel as Eidos theou ("Form of God," and "the Form of God" in 32:32), preserving a Greek wordplay with eidon ("I have seen") in the clause that follows.
notes.33:10: The Greek reads the future indicative ("and you will be pleased with me"), whereas the Hebrew has a past verb ("and you have received me favorably").
notes.33:17: The Greek translates the Hebrew place name Succoth as Skenai ("Booths" or "Tents"), preserving the wordplay with the booths Jacob made for his livestock.
notes.33:18: The Greek takes Hebrew shalem ("safely") as a place name, "Salem, a city of Shechem," and renders Paddan-aram as "Mesopotamia of Syria."
notes.33:19: The Greek translates the rare Hebrew unit qesitah as amnon ("lambs"), reading "one hundred lambs."
notes.34:2: The Greek text reads "the Horite" (ho Chorraios), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Hivite."
notes.34:14: The Septuagint explicitly names "Simeon and Levi, the brothers of Dinah and sons of Leah" as the speakers, whereas the Masoretic Text refers generally to the sons of Jacob.
notes.34:29: Greek somata ("persons") is a common Hellenistic term for captives or household servants, and aposkeue ("household goods") frequently translates the Hebrew word for dependents or little ones.
notes.35:4: The Septuagint includes the final clause "and destroyed them until this day," which is absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.35:8: The Greek text omits "and she was buried," explicitly names Jacob as the one who named the tree, and translates the Hebrew name Allon-bacuth as "Oak of Mourning."
notes.35:11: The Septuagint reads "I am your God" rather than Hebrew El Shaddai ("God Almighty"), and uses plural "nations and assemblies of nations."
notes.35:16: The Septuagint incorporates the tent pitched beyond the tower of Gader (MT "Eder" in 35:21) here, so verse 35:21 is absent in Greek; "Chabratha" transliterates a Hebrew term for a stretch of distance.
notes.35:22: The Septuagint includes "and it appeared evil before him" after "Israel heard," completing the well-known mid-verse break in the Masoretic Text.
notes.35:27: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew place name Kiriath-arba as "the city of the plain" (polin tou pediou).
notes.36:2: The Greek text reads "Anah the son of Zibeon" (also in 36:14), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "daughter of Zibeon," and it names the Hittite father Elom (Hebrew Elon).
notes.36:21: The Greek names the last two Horite chiefs Saar and Rison (Hebrew Ezer and Dishan), and likewise preserves distinct proper-name forms elsewhere in the chapter, including Sophar (36:11), Nahom and Masemath (36:13), Jeul (36:18), and four sons of Saar (36:27).
notes.36:24: The Greek treats the obscure Hebrew word often translated "hot springs" as a proper name, "Jamin," and names the finder Onan/Onas (Hebrew Anah).
notes.36:31: This Greek text reads "in Jerusalem," where the Masoretic Text reads "over the children of Israel."
notes.36:39: The Greek names the king "Harath the son of Barath" (Hebrew "Hadar," without a father's name), calls his city Phogor (Hebrew Pau), and reads "Matraith the son of Mezoob" (Hebrew "Matred, daughter of Mezahab"); similar Greek-distinct names appear in 36:32–36 (Balak, Jobad, Barad, Gethaim, Salama, Masekka) and 36:40–43 (Gola, Jeber, Phines, Mazar, Metodiel, Zaphoei).
notes.37:2: The Greek uses a plural verb ("they brought") with Joseph as object, stating that Joseph's brothers brought an evil report against him to Israel, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text makes Joseph the one bringing an evil report about them.
notes.37:28: The Greek reads "twenty pieces of gold," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "twenty pieces of silver."
notes.37:34: The Greek text here reads "for some days," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (and many Greek manuscripts) reads "for many days."
notes.37:36: The Greek renders Potiphar's titles literally as "eunuch" and "chief cook," reflecting the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew court titles often translated "officer" and "captain of the guard."
notes.38:2: In the Greek text the feminine relative pronoun makes Shua the name of Judah's wife herself (as also in verse 12), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text identifies Shua as her father.
notes.38:5: The Greek reads "she was in Chezib when she bore them," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to Judah ("he") being at Chezib when she bore Shelah ("him").
notes.38:12: Here and in verse 20, the Greek identifies Hirah as Judah's "shepherd," reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic reading "friend."
notes.38:14: The Greek renders the place name as Enan (compare Hebrew "Enaim") and states that Tamar "adorned herself."
notes.39:1: The Greek renders Potiphar (Πετεφρῆς) as Pharaoh's "eunuch" (εὐνοῦχος) and "chief cook" (ἀρχιμάγειρος), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text designates him an officer and captain of the guard.
notes.39:4: The Greek reads "he was pleasing to him" (εὐηρέστει δὲ αὐτῷ), rather than "he served him" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.39:8: The Greek opens Joseph's reply with a conditional "If" (Εἰ) and reads "because of me" (δι᾽ ἐμέ), linking verses 8 and 9 into a single sentence.
notes.39:20: The Greek terms the royal prison "the stronghold" (τὸ ὀχύρωμα; also in 40:14) and includes the concluding phrase "there in the stronghold."
notes.40:4: The Greek uses the rare title ἀρχιδεσμώτης (here rendered "chief jailer") in place of ἀρχιδεσμοφύλαξ used in 39:21–23 and 40:3.
notes.40:5: The Greek reads "a vision of his own dream" (ὅρασις τοῦ ἐνυπνίου αὐτοῦ), contrasting with "according to the interpretation of his dream" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.40:13: The Greek renders the Hebrew idiom "lift up your head" as "remember your office" (μνησθήσεται ... τῆς ἀρχῆς σου; likewise in 40:20).
notes.40:16: The Greek specifies "coarse-wheat loaves" (χονδριτῶν), bread made from groats, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to white or wicker baskets.
notes.41:16: The Greek literally reads 'Apart from God, no answer of welfare (or deliverance) shall be given to Pharaoh,' expressing Joseph's dependence on God in a different construction from the Hebrew ('It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace').
notes.41:45: The Greek preserves the Septuagint form Psonthomphanech for Joseph's Egyptian name (Hebrew 'Zaphnath-paaneah'), spells Potiphera as Petrephes (Petrephe), and renders the Egyptian city of On by its Greek name Heliopolis ('City of the Sun').
notes.41:48: This Greek text uniquely includes the proper name 'On' (the Egyptian name for Heliopolis) in describing the grain stored from the surrounding fields.
notes.41:52: This Greek reading has 'exalted me' (hypsosen) rather than 'increased me' (standard Septuagint) or 'made me fruitful' (Hebrew), sharpening the contrast with 'the land of my humiliation.'
notes.41:54: This Greek text reads 'there was no bread' in Egypt (in contrast to the Hebrew Masoretic Text, 'there was bread'), directly anticipating the people's cry for bread in verse 55.
notes.42:1: The Septuagint reads "selling" (prasis) rather than "grain," and "Why are you idle?" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Why do you look at one another?"
notes.42:4: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew word for "harm" as "sickness" (malakia), corresponding to "fall sick" (malakisthenai) in 42:38.
notes.42:9: "The tracks of the country" (ta ichne, also "tracks of the land" in 42:12) is the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew idiom "the nakedness of the land," referring to its vulnerable approaches.
notes.42:20: The Septuagint concludes Joseph's condition with a warning ("otherwise, you shall die"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "and you shall not die."
notes.42:38: "Hades" translates the Greek Hades, the standard Septuagint rendering of Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead.
notes.43:14: The Septuagint reads "my God" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "God Almighty" (El Shaddai), and "your one brother" rather than "your other brother."
notes.43:23: "Mercy be to you" renders the Greek idiom hileos hymin (literally "gracious to you," an elliptic invocation of divine favor), corresponding to Hebrew "Peace be to you."
notes.43:28: The Septuagint includes Joseph's blessing, "Blessed is that man by God," which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.43:32: The Septuagint specifies that "every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians" (cf. 46:34), expanding the shorter reading of the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("for that is an abomination to the Egyptians").
notes.44:4: The Greek text includes the additional question "Why have you stolen my silver cup?"—whose Greek interrogative phrase is split across the boundary of verses 4 and 5—which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.44:18: The Greek reads "you are next after Pharaoh" (literally "after Pharaoh"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "you are like Pharaoh."
notes.44:20: The Greek reads "he alone was left to his father," contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "of his mother."
notes.44:29: The Greek renders the Hebrew term for harm as "infirmity" (sickness) and uses "old age" and "Hades" where the Hebrew has gray hair and Sheol.
notes.45:3: In the Greek text, Joseph identifies himself as "your brother, whom you sold into Egypt" already in verse 3 as well as in verse 4, and verse 4 omits the command to come near found in the Hebrew.
notes.45:10: The Greek reads "Gesem of Arabia" (rendered here as "Goshen of Arabia"), identifying Goshen with the Arabian district of eastern Egypt.
notes.45:14: The Greek text here reads "he fell upon him" rather than "he wept," while stating that Benjamin wept upon Joseph's neck.
notes.45:22: The Greek specifies "three hundred pieces of gold" given to Benjamin, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text specifies pieces of silver.
notes.46:1: "The Well of the Oath" translates Greek to phrear tou horkou, the Septuagint's literal rendering of the Hebrew place name Beersheba.
notes.46:10: Several genealogical names in vv. 9–24 preserve distinct Septuagint forms differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, including Phallud (MT Pallu), Jachim (MT Jachin), Samuel (MT Shaul), Shelom (MT Shelah), Jemuel in v. 12 (MT Hamul), Jasuph and Zambram (MT Job and Shimron), Hasron in v. 14 (MT Elon), Thasoban and Aedis (MT Ezbon and Eri), Jessai, Jeul, and Saar (MT Ishvah, Ishvi, and Serah), Chobor and Anchis (MT Becher and Ehi), and Issaar (MT Jezer).
notes.46:20: "Heliopolis" translates Greek Heliou polis (City of the Sun), the Septuagint name for Hebrew On. The Septuagint also records additional descendants of Manasseh and Ephraim (Machir, Gilead, Sutalaam, Taam, and Edem) not listed here in the Masoretic Text.
notes.46:27: In keeping with the expanded genealogy of v. 20, the Septuagint counts nine sons born to Joseph in Egypt and a total of seventy-five souls of the house of Jacob entering Egypt (matching Acts 7:14), whereas the Masoretic Text reads two and seventy.
notes.46:28: "Heroopolis" (Heroon polis) is the Septuagint place name in vv. 28–29 where the Masoretic Text has Goshen; in v. 34, the Septuagint likewise specifies "the land of Goshen of Arabia."
notes.47:5: This Septuagint versification combines the material of vv. 4–5 (with no separate v. 4) and places Pharaoh's grant of Goshen ahead of the notice that Jacob and his sons came to Egypt.
notes.47:19: The Greek text here omits a negative before "will become desolate" (kai he ge eremothesetai), whereas the Masoretic Text and some Greek witnesses read "and the land will not become desolate."
notes.47:21: The Septuagint reads "enslaved the people to him as servants" (agreeing with the Samaritan Pentateuch), whereas the Masoretic Text reads that Joseph moved the people into cities.
notes.47:31: The Septuagint reads "upon the top of his staff" (quoted in Hebrews 11:21), whereas the Masoretic Text vocalizes the Hebrew word to mean "the head of the bed."
notes.48:3: The Greek reads "my God" (ho theos mou) rather than the Hebrew Masoretic "God Almighty" (El Shaddai).
notes.48:7: The Greek renders the Hebrew measure of distance both as "hippodrome" (racecourse) and by transliterating it as "Chabratha," and reads "Mesopotamia of Syria" where the Hebrew has "Paddan."
notes.48:15: The Greek reads "blessed them" and "the Lord" (ho kyrios) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "blessed Joseph" and "the God."
notes.48:22: The Greek treats the Hebrew word for "ridge" or "portion" (shekhem) as the city name Sikima (Shechem), pairing it with a feminine relative pronoun ("which I took").
notes.49:5: The Greek reads "they accomplished injustice by their own choice," differing notably from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's reference to weapons of violence.
notes.49:6: The Greek reads "my liver" (ta hepata mou, a seat of passion in ancient idiom) and "not contend," reflecting a different reading from the Hebrew Masoretic "my glory" and "not be united."
notes.49:10: The Greek interprets the difficult Hebrew term Shiloh as "the things laid up for him" (ta apokeimena auto) and concludes "he is the expectation of the nations."
notes.49:18: Rather than an abrupt first-person exclamation as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Greek uses a participle ("awaiting the salvation of the Lord") that directly continues the saying about Dan in verse 17.
notes.49:22: The Greek oracle for Joseph differs substantially from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, describing him as "my envied son increased" and ending with an appeal, "my youngest son, return to me."
notes.50:2: The Greek designates Joseph's servants specifically as "embalmers" (entaphiastai), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "physicians."
notes.50:11: The Greek translates the place name as "Mourning of Egypt" (Penthos Aigyptou), rendering the Hebrew name Abel-mizraim.
notes.50:13: The Greek renders the Hebrew name Machpelah descriptively as "the double cave" (to spelaion to diploun) and does not mention the field alongside the cave.
notes.50:19: The Greek reads as a direct declaration, "for I belong to God," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text poses a rhetorical question ("Am I in the place of God?").
notes.50:26: The Greek verb used here (thapto, ordinarily "bury") carries its Ptolemaic Egyptian sense of preparing a body by embalming prior to placing it in a coffin, matching "embalming" (taphe) in verse 3.
